critical_questions.label: CQ1
critical_questions.text: Is a in a position to know whether A is true (false)?
critical_questions.reason: Restates the major premise (the proponent must show it). The book says this CQ 'is directed against the major premise: if the source is not in a position to know, the whole argument collapses' (p. 89-90).
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 17: CQ1 and P1 'are closely related and might be characterized as a single premise'.

critical_questions.label: CQ2
critical_questions.text: Is a an honest (trustworthy, reliable) source?
critical_questions.reason: Whoever alleges dishonesty must back it up. The book says this of the parallel trustworthiness question for expert opinion (p. 33: without evidence the question 'is merely an innuendo').
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 17: 'for an argument from position to know to be successful, it is necessary for an audience to accept that a is honest'; CQ2 'is clearly distinct and forms a second premise'. p. 90: the assertion 'may be unreliable because the source is dishonest'.

critical_questions.label: CQ3
critical_questions.text: Did a assert that A is true (false)?
critical_questions.reason: Restates the minor premise (that a asserted A).
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 17: P2 and CQ3 are similar, but CQ3 is 'aiming for the very words a spoke, as opposed to a paraphrasing or interpretation'. p. 90: 'his words have been distorted'.

premises.label: Major Premise
premises.text: Source E is an expert in subject domain S containing proposition A.

premises.label: Minor Premise
premises.text: E asserts that proposition A (in domain S) is true (false).

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: A may plausibly be taken to be true (false).

critical_questions.label: 1. Expertise Question
critical_questions.text: How credible is E as an expert source?
critical_questions.reason: Proponent's burden: 'you assume, as part of the argument, that the source is credible' (p. 33). Covered by the major premise (Expertise Premise in version IV).
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 33: CQs 1, 2, 3 and 6 'can be seen as implicit premises' (merely asking makes the argument default; the burden stays on the proponent); 4 and 5 'seem to have a positive burden of proof attached to the side of the questioner'.
critical_questions.variant_wording: p. 32: 'How credible (knowledgeable) is E as an expert source?'

critical_questions.label: 2. Field Question
critical_questions.text: Is E an expert in the field that A is in?
critical_questions.reason: Proponent's burden (p. 33: 'You assume that the expert is an expert in the field of the claim made'). Covered by the major premise ('domain S containing proposition A'); Field Premise in version IV.
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 27: in the Bradshaw example the field CQ and the domain variable S diagnose the same fault twice ('a kind of duplication').

critical_questions.label: 3. Opinion Question
critical_questions.text: What did E assert that implies A?
critical_questions.reason: Proponent's burden (p. 33: the expert 'has said something ... from which the claim can be extracted'). Covered by the minor premise; Opinion Premise in version IV.

critical_questions.label: 4. Trustworthiness Question
critical_questions.text: Is E personally reliable as a source?
critical_questions.reason: Questioner's burden: 'to mount such an attack, the critic has to produce some fairly substantial evidence. Otherwise, the question is merely an innuendo' (p. 33).
critical_questions.book_comment: Subquestions (Walton, 1997, p. 217), p. 31: 'Subquestion 1: Is E biased? / Subquestion 2: Is E honest? / Subquestion 3: Is E conscientious?'
critical_questions.variant_wording: p. 33: 'Is E personally reliable as a source – for example, is E biased?'

critical_questions.label: 5. Consistency Question
critical_questions.text: Is A consistent with what other experts assert?
critical_questions.reason: Questioner's burden: 'that needs to be shown by telling us what the other experts have in fact said' (p. 33).
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 33: 'then that is an argument against the claim. It is a rebuttal, especially if what the other experts say represents the generally accepted opinion in the field.' See also p. 92 under CQ 6.

critical_questions.label: 6. Backup Evidence Question
critical_questions.text: Is E's assertion based on evidence?
critical_questions.reason: Proponent's burden: 'You assume that the expert's assertion was based on some evidence within the field of his or her expertise' (p. 33). Not among the premises of versions I/II (Backup Evidence Premise in IV).
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 92: 'The last two questions [5 and 6] are directed against the plausibility of the link between premises and conclusion ... Both these attacks weaken the acceptability of the conclusion, but they do not compromise the argument's validity.'

wag_cq_comparison.note: Two wording differences. The book compares with other experts, WAG with other credible sources. The book asks whether A is CONSISTENT with them, WAG whether they AGREE. Sources can be consistent with A by saying nothing about it, so a 'no' to WAG's question need not mean that they disagree. Yet WAG's exception pattern is other_credible_sources_disagree({S}). Both treat the CQ as an exception. The book (p. 33) also calls it 'a rebuttal', so conclusion is the alternative.

wag_cq_comparison.note: The meaning is the same. The loci differ. WAG uses argument (an undercutter). On p. 33 the book treats this CQ as an implicit premise, i.e. an assumption the proponent must support. On p. 92 it groups CQs 5 and 6 as attacks on 'the link between premises and conclusion', which supports WAG's choice. The two passages disagree.

wag_cq_comparison.note: There are 21 subquestions on pp. 92-93, and 4.1-4.3 are also printed on p. 31. WAG has none; they could serve as finer CQ nodes or as hints.

wag_premise_comparison: Major premise. Book: 'Source E is an expert in subject domain S containing proposition A.' WAG: '{W} is a credible expert on {D}', plus a separate premise '{S} is a matter of {D}'. WAG folds the Expertise CQ ('credible') into the premise and splits off domain membership. The split matches version IV, which has separate Expertise and Field Premises.
Minor premise. Book: 'E asserts that proposition A (in domain S) is true (false).' WAG: '{W} says that {S}'. WAG drops the negative reading, '(false)'.
The variable letters clash. In the book S is the DOMAIN and A the proposition; in WAG S is the proposition and D the domain.

WAG's carneades_id is credible_source (Wyner 2016), not walton.yml expert_opinion (Walton 1997). expert_opinion's loci follow the book's p. 33 burdens one to one, with based_on_evidence as an assumption.
mapping.wag_conclusion_comparison: Book (1997): 'A may plausibly be taken to be true (false).' Book (2002, p. 91): 'A is true (false).' WAG: '{S}'. WAG drops 'plausibly' and the (false) form.
mapping.walton_yml_note: walton.yml expert_opinion (source Walton 1997, pp. 211-225): expert(W,D), in_domain(S,D), asserts(W,S); exceptions untrustworthy(W), inconsistent_with_other_experts(S); assumption based_on_evidence(asserts(W,S)). Its loci match the book's p. 33 burdens one to one. WAG's AS:expert_opinion instead uses credible_source (Wyner 2016).

critical_questions.text: Is there some other case C3 that is also similar to C1 except that A is false (true) in C3?
critical_questions.reason: Points to a counteranalogy, an argument for the opposite conclusion (a rebuttal).
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 63: 'CQ4 looks more like a defeater ... The strategy for attacking an argument from analogy suggested by CQ4 is to produce a counteranalogy ... This attack would seem to be a defeater.'

premises.text: If some particular thing a can be classified as falling under verbal category C, then a has property F (in virtue of such a classification).

premises.label: Minor Premise
premises.text: a can be classified as falling under verbal category C.

critical_questions.label: CQ1
critical_questions.text: Does a definitely have F, or is there room for doubt?
critical_questions.reason: Raises doubt about whether the generalization carries over to this case, without a statement behind it (an undercutter).

critical_questions.reason: Explicitly targets the second (minor) premise.

schemes.book_name: Scheme for Argument from an Established Rule
schemes.chapter: 2. Argumentation Schemes for Arguments from Analogy, Classification, and Precedent
schemes.section: 7. Arguments Based on Rules and Classifications

premises.label: Major Premise
premises.text: If carrying out types of actions including the state of affairs A is the established rule for x, then (unless the case is an exception), x must carry out A.

premises.label: Minor Premise
premises.text: Carrying out types of actions including the state of affairs A is the established rule for a.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Therefore, a must carry out A.

critical_questions.label: CQ1
critical_questions.text: Does the rule require carrying out types of actions that include A as an instance?
critical_questions.reason: Questions what the rule requires, i.e. the minor premise and the major premise's antecedent (proponent's burden).

critical_questions.label: CQ2
critical_questions.text: Are there other established rules that might conflict with, or override, this one?
critical_questions.reason: The questioner must cite the conflicting rule.

critical_questions.label: CQ3
critical_questions.text: Is this case an exceptional one, that is, could there be extenuating circumstances or an excuse for noncompliance?
critical_questions.reason: The major premise itself reserves '(unless the case is an exception)'; the questioner must cite the excuse (cf. Argument from an Exceptional Case, S21).
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 71: 'The last critical question concerns the problem of the exceptional case ... The counterargument is a kind of rebuttal of the implicit assumption that the case in question represents an instance of the rule.'

schemes.cq_source: heading 'Critical Questions for Argument from an Established Rule'

mapping.walton_yml_note: walton.yml established_rule (source Walton 1995, p. 147): has_conclusion(R,C), applicable(R); assumption valid(R). Generic rule application, no exception formula; regulative_rule (Grennan) has a 0-ary exception excuse.

notes: p. 71: 'The critical questions are directed against the generalization in the rule.'
It 'belongs to a different kind of dialogue, that of deliberation' (p. 71).

premises.label: Major Premise
premises.text: If the case of x is an exception, then the established rule can be waived in the case of x.

premises.label: Minor Premise
premises.text: The case of a is an exception.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Therefore, the established rule can be waived in the case of a.

critical_questions.label: CQ1
critical_questions.text: Is the case of a a recognized type of exception?
critical_questions.reason: Questions the minor premise.

critical_questions.label: CQ2
critical_questions.text: If it is not a recognized case, can evidence why the established rule does not apply to it be given?
critical_questions.reason: Asks the proponent for evidence for the minor premise when the exception is not a recognized type.

critical_questions.label: CQ3
critical_questions.text: If it is a borderline case, can comparable cases be cited?
critical_questions.reason: Asks the proponent to support a borderline exception with comparable cases (argument from analogy).
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 72: 'The last critical question indicates how argument from an exceptional case and its rebuttals are based on argument from analogy'.

schemes.cq_source: heading 'Critical Questions for Argument from an Exceptional Case'

notes: p. 72: 'The critical questions stem from the classification.'

premises.label: Major Premise
premises.text: Generally, according to the established rule, if x has property F, then x also has property G.

premises.text: In this legitimate case, a has property F but does not have property G.

conclusion.text: Therefore, an exception to the rule must be recognized, and the rule must be appropriately modified or qualified.

critical_questions.label: CQ1
critical_questions.text: Does the established rule really apply to this case?
critical_questions.reason: Questions the minor premise (that the cited case falls under the rule).

critical_questions.label: CQ2
critical_questions.text: Is the case cited legitimate, or can it be explained as only an apparent violation of the rule?
critical_questions.reason: Questions 'In this legitimate case' in the minor premise.

critical_questions.label: CQ3
critical_questions.text: Can the case cited be dealt with under an already recognized category of exception that does not require a change in the rule?
critical_questions.reason: The defender of the rule cites an existing exception category; the premises stand but the conclusion (modify the rule) is blocked.

schemes.name_from: text: 'The argument from position to know takes the following form (Walton, 2002, p. 46)'
schemes.chapter: 3. Knowledge-Related, Practical, and Other Schemes

premises.label: Major Premise
premises.text: Source a is in a position to know about things in a certain subject domain S containing proposition A.

premises.label: Minor Premise
premises.text: a asserts that A is true (false).

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: A is true (false).

critical_questions.label: CQ1
critical_questions.text: Is a in a position to know whether A is true (false)?
critical_questions.reason: Restates the major premise (the proponent must show it). The book says this CQ 'is directed against the major premise: if the source is not in a position to know, the whole argument collapses' (p. 89-90).
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 17: CQ1 and P1 'are closely related and might be characterized as a single premise'.

critical_questions.label: CQ2
critical_questions.text: Is a an honest (trustworthy, reliable) source?
critical_questions.reason: Whoever alleges dishonesty must back it up. The book says this of the parallel trustworthiness question for expert opinion (p. 33: without evidence the question 'is merely an innuendo').
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 17: 'for an argument from position to know to be successful, it is necessary for an audience to accept that a is honest'; CQ2 'is clearly distinct and forms a second premise'. p. 90: the assertion 'may be unreliable because the source is dishonest'.

critical_questions.label: CQ3
critical_questions.text: Did a assert that A is true (false)?
critical_questions.reason: Restates the minor premise (that a asserted A).
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 17: P2 and CQ3 are similar, but CQ3 is 'aiming for the very words a spoke, as opposed to a paraphrasing or interpretation'. p. 90: 'his words have been distorted'.

notes: Differs from p. 13 only in the minor premise ('a asserts that A is true (false).' without '(in domain S)').

p. 89-90: 'The first critical question is directed against the major premise: if the source is not in a position to know, the whole argument collapses. The remaining two critical questions focus on the problem of the assertion: it may be unreliable because the source is dishonest, or because his words have been distorted.'

schemes.name_from: text: 'The following scheme represents the general form of the argument from witness testimony (Prakken, Reed, and Walton, 2003, p. 35)'
schemes.chapter: 3. Knowledge-Related, Practical, and Other Schemes

premises.label: Position-to-Know Premise
premises.text: Witness W is in position to know whether A is true or not.

premises.label: Truth-Telling Premise
premises.text: Witness W is telling the truth (as W knows it).

premises.label: Statement Premise
premises.text: Witness W states that A is true (false).

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: A may be plausibly taken to be true (false).

critical_questions.label: CQ1
critical_questions.text: Is what the witness said internally consistent?
critical_questions.reason: Checkable from the testimony itself; the proponent offering the testimony can be expected to show it hangs together.

critical_questions.label: CQ2
critical_questions.text: Is what the witness said consistent with the known facts of the case (based on evidence apart from what the witness testified to)?
critical_questions.reason: The questioner must cite the conflicting facts.

critical_questions.label: CQ3
critical_questions.text: Is what the witness said consistent with what other witnesses have (independently) testified to?
critical_questions.reason: The questioner must cite the conflicting testimony.

critical_questions.label: CQ4
critical_questions.text: Is there some kind of bias that can be attributed to the account given by the witness?
critical_questions.reason: Bias has to be shown by evidence (cf. p. 33 on trustworthiness).

critical_questions.label: CQ5
critical_questions.text: How plausible is the statement A asserted by the witness?
critical_questions.reason: Evidence that A is implausible is evidence against A itself (a rebuttal).

mapping.walton_yml_note: walton.yml witness_testimony: position_to_know(W,D), in_domain(D,S) [arguments reversed vs. other schemes], believes(W,S), asserts(W,S); assumption internally_consistent(S) (CQ1); exceptions inconsistent_with_known_facts(S) (CQ2), inconsistent_with_other_witnesses(S) (CQ3), biased(W) (CQ4), implausible(S) (CQ5). Its loci match the drafts here except CQ5 (exception there, conclusion here).

notes: p. 90-91: 'The reliability of the source being the most important condition of the scheme, the critical questions are directed against this major premise. Consistency of the statement with the rest of the testimony, with the known facts, and with other testimony, along with source bias, are the most important factors used to evaluate the trustworthiness of the witness and, consequently, the plausibility of his statement.'
p. 90: 'The truth-telling premise is an important difference from the previous scheme.'

schemes.name_from: text: 'This is the form of the argument from expert opinion (Walton, 2002, p. 50)'
schemes.chapter: 3. Knowledge-Related, Practical, and Other Schemes

premises.label: Major Premise
premises.text: Source E is an expert in subject domain S containing proposition A.

premises.label: Minor Premise
premises.text: E asserts that proposition A is true (false).

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: A is true (false).

critical_questions.label: 1. Expertise Question
critical_questions.text: How credible is E as an expert source?
critical_questions.reason: Proponent's burden: 'you assume, as part of the argument, that the source is credible' (p. 33). Covered by the major premise (Expertise Premise in version IV).
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 33: CQs 1, 2, 3 and 6 'can be seen as implicit premises' (merely asking makes the argument default; the burden stays on the proponent); 4 and 5 'seem to have a positive burden of proof attached to the side of the questioner'.
critical_questions.variant_wording: p. 32: 'How credible (knowledgeable) is E as an expert source?'

subquestions.text: What is E's name, job or official capacity, location, and employer?
What degrees, professional qualifications, or certification by licensing agencies does E hold?
Can testimony of peer experts in the same field be given to support E's competence?
What is E's record of experience or other indications of practiced skill in S?
What is E's record of peer-reviewed publications or contributions to knowledge in S?

critical_questions.label: 2. Field Question
critical_questions.text: Is E an expert in the field that A is in?
critical_questions.reason: Proponent's burden (p. 33: 'You assume that the expert is an expert in the field of the claim made'). Covered by the major premise ('domain S containing proposition A'); Field Premise in version IV.
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 27: in the Bradshaw example the field CQ and the domain variable S diagnose the same fault twice ('a kind of duplication').

subquestions.text: Is the field of expertise cited in the appeal a genuine area of knowledge or an area of technical skill that supports a claim to knowledge?
If E is an expert in a field closely related to the field cited in the appeal, how close is the relationship between the expertise in the two fields?
Is the issue one where expert knowledge in any field is directly relevant to deciding the issue?
Is the field of expertise cited an area where there are changes in techniques or rapid developments in new knowledge? If so, is the expert up to date in these developments?

critical_questions.label: 3. Opinion Question
critical_questions.text: What did E assert that implies A?
critical_questions.reason: Proponent's burden (p. 33: the expert 'has said something ... from which the claim can be extracted'). Covered by the minor premise; Opinion Premise in version IV.

subquestions.text: Was E quoted as asserting A? Was a reference to the source of the quote given, and can it be verified that E actually said A?
If E did not say A exactly, then what did E assert, and how was A inferred?

If the inference to A was based on more than one premise, could one premise have come from E and the other from a different expert? If so, is there evidence of disagreement between what the two experts (separately) asserted?

Is what E asserted clear? If not, was the process of interpretation of what A said by the respondent who used E's opinion justified? Are other interpretations plausible? Could important qualifications have been left out?

critical_questions.label: 4. Trustworthiness Question
critical_questions.text: Is E personally reliable as a source?
critical_questions.reason: Questioner's burden: 'to mount such an attack, the critic has to produce some fairly substantial evidence. Otherwise, the question is merely an innuendo' (p. 33).
critical_questions.book_comment: Subquestions (Walton, 1997, p. 217), p. 31: 'Subquestion 1: Is E biased? / Subquestion 2: Is E honest? / Subquestion 3: Is E conscientious?'
critical_questions.variant_wording: p. 33: 'Is E personally reliable as a source – for example, is E biased?'

subquestions.text: Is E biased?
Is E honest?
Is E conscientious?

critical_questions.label: 5. Consistency Question
critical_questions.text: Is A consistent with what other experts assert?
critical_questions.reason: Questioner's burden: 'that needs to be shown by telling us what the other experts have in fact said' (p. 33).
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 33: 'then that is an argument against the claim. It is a rebuttal, especially if what the other experts say represents the generally accepted opinion in the field.' See also p. 92 under CQ 6.

subquestions.text: Does A have general acceptance in S?
If not, can E explain why not, and give reasons why there is good evidence for A?

critical_questions.label: 6. Backup Evidence Question
critical_questions.text: Is E's assertion based on evidence?
critical_questions.reason: Proponent's burden: 'You assume that the expert's assertion was based on some evidence within the field of his or her expertise' (p. 33). Not among the premises of versions I/II (Backup Evidence Premise in IV).
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 92: 'The last two questions [5 and 6] are directed against the plausibility of the link between premises and conclusion ... Both these attacks weaken the acceptability of the conclusion, but they do not compromise the argument's validity.'

subquestions.text: What is the internal evidence the expert herself used to arrive at this opinion as her conclusion?
If there is external evidence (e.g., physical evidence reported independently of the expert), can the expert deal with this adequately?
Can it be shown that the opinion given is one that is scientifically verifiable?

notes: Differs from S03: minor premise without '(in domain S)', conclusion 'A is true (false).' instead of 'A may plausibly be taken to be true (false).'
Subquestion 3.4 is printed 'what A said' (sic; E is meant).

p. 92: 'the trustworthiness attack undermines the argument on the basis of source bias or dishonesty.' p. 92: 'The last two questions [5 and 6] are directed against the plausibility of the link between premises and conclusion ... Both these attacks weaken the acceptability of the conclusion, but they do not compromise the argument's validity.'

schemes.book_name: argumentation scheme for practical reasoning (Goal Premise / Means Premise)
schemes.name_from: text: 'In the argumentation scheme for practical reasoning presented here ...'
schemes.chapter: 3. Knowledge-Related, Practical, and Other Schemes

premises.label: Goal Premise
premises.text: Bringing about Sₙ is my goal.

premises.label: Means Premise
premises.text: In order to bring about Sₙ, I need to bring about Sᵢ.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Therefore, I need to bring about Sᵢ.

variables: S₀, S₁, . . . Sₙ (states of affairs, ordered temporally)

critical_questions.label: Other-Means Question
critical_questions.text: Are there alternative possible actions to bring about Sᵢ that could also lead to the goal?
critical_questions.reason: The questioner has to name the alternative; its existence does not follow from the premises.
critical_questions.book_comment: p. 96: 'Asking any one of these five critical questions can defeat the argumentation, at least temporarily. Once the proponent gives an adequate answer to the question, however, the burden shifts back to the respondent.' Read literally, that treats all five as burdens on the proponent (premise/assumption). In the necessary/sufficient schemata the Alternatives and Selection Premises (N2, N3 / S2, S3) state what this CQ asks.

critical_questions.label: Best-Means Question
critical_questions.text: Is Sᵢ the best (or most favorable) of the alternatives?
critical_questions.reason: The questioner must show a better alternative.
critical_questions.book_comment: Stated as the Selection Premise (N3/S3: 'the most acceptable ... condition') in the schemata.

critical_questions.label: Other-Goals Question
critical_questions.text: Do I have goals other than Sᵢ whose achievement is preferable and that should have priority?
critical_questions.reason: Points to a counterargument: practical reasoning from a goal with priority, against bringing about Sᵢ.
critical_questions.book_comment: As printed, 'goals other than Sᵢ' (Sᵢ is the means, Sₙ the goal). In two-person practical reasoning the matching CQ1 speaks of goals 'that might conflict with the goal of realizing A' (p. 97).

critical_questions.label: Possibility Question
critical_questions.text: Is it possible to bring about Sᵢ in the given circumstances?
critical_questions.reason: Proponent's burden; not stated in the Goal/Means scheme. In the schemata it is the Practicality Premise (N4/S4).

critical_questions.label: Side Effects Question
critical_questions.text: Would bringing about Sᵢ have known bad consequences that ought to be taken into account?
critical_questions.reason: The questioner must cite the known bad consequences.

wag_premise_comparison: This is a different scheme. WAG's carneades_id practical_reasoning1 is Atkinson & Bench-Capon's value-based scheme. Its four premises are: the current situation is S1; doing A in S1 would lead to S2; goal G would be achieved in S2; achieving G would promote value V.

The excerpt states Walton's goal/means scheme instead (p. 95): 'Goal Premise: Bringing about Sₙ is my goal.' / 'Means Premise: In order to bring about Sₙ, I need to bring about Sᵢ.' It also gives the five-premise necessary- and sufficient-condition schemata (pp. 95-96), with Goal, Alternatives, Selection, Practicality and Side-Effects premises.

The book has no circumstances premise and no value premise. The value-related formulas in core.yml have no counterpart in the excerpt: would_promote_value, the assumptions legitimate_value(V) and worthy_goal(G), and the exception promote_more_effectively(V,A).
The book's agent speaks in the first person ('my goal', 'I need to').
WAG does not represent the book's distinction between Bᵢ as a necessary condition and Bᵢ as a sufficient condition.
mapping.wag_conclusion_comparison: WAG: '{A} should be done'. Book: 'Therefore, I need to bring about Sᵢ.', a 'practical ought' (p. 95); the N-schema has 'Therefore, it is required that I bring about Bᵢ.' The S-schema prints no conclusion.
wag_other_differences: p. 96: 'Asking any one of these five critical questions can defeat the argumentation, at least temporarily. Once the proponent gives an adequate answer ... the burden shifts back to the respondent.' This passage treats all five CQs as putting the burden on the proponent, i.e. as premises or assumptions. WAG, like Carneades, makes three of them exceptions; the excerpt does not settle which reading is right.
No book CQ corresponds to the core.yml assumptions legitimate_value(V) and worthy_goal(G) or to the exception promote_more_effectively(V,A). WAG has no CQ edges to them either.
mapping.walton_yml_note: walton.yml practical_inference (sources Walton 1990, 1997 p. 164): have_goal(G), action_realize_goal(A,G) -> carry_out_action(A); exceptions other_goals_conflict(G), more_efficient_alternative_actions(A,G), incompatible_consequences(A,G); assumptions possible_action(A), possible_goal(G). Closest to this scheme and its five CQs. practical_reasoning2 (instrumental, Walton 2015) is related; practical_reasoning1 (WAG's) is the value-based Atkinson & Bench-Capon scheme, not in the excerpt.

premises: This is a different scheme. WAG's carneades_id practical_reasoning1 is Atkinson & Bench-Capon's value-based scheme. Its four premises are: the current situation is S1; doing A in S1 would lead to S2; goal G would be achieved in S2; achieving G would promote value V.

The excerpt states Walton's goal/means scheme instead (p. 95): 'Goal Premise: Bringing about Sₙ is my goal.' / 'Means Premise: In order to bring about Sₙ, I need to bring about Sᵢ.' It also gives the five-premise necessary- and sufficient-condition schemata (pp. 95-96), with Goal, Alternatives, Selection, Practicality and Side-Effects premises.

The book has no circumstances premise and no value premise. The value-related formulas in core.yml have no counterpart in the excerpt: would_promote_value, the assumptions legitimate_value(V) and worthy_goal(G), and the exception promote_more_effectively(V,A).
The book's agent speaks in the first person ('my goal', 'I need to').
WAG does not represent the book's distinction between Bᵢ as a necessary condition and Bᵢ as a sufficient condition.
AS:practical_reasoning.conclusion: WAG: '{A} should be done'. Book: 'Therefore, I need to bring about Sᵢ.', a 'practical ought' (p. 95); the N-schema has 'Therefore, it is required that I bring about Bᵢ.' The S-schema prints no conclusion.
other: p. 96: 'Asking any one of these five critical questions can defeat the argumentation, at least temporarily. Once the proponent gives an adequate answer ... the burden shifts back to the respondent.' This passage treats all five CQs as putting the burden on the proponent, i.e. as premises or assumptions. WAG, like Carneades, makes three of them exceptions; the excerpt does not settle which reading is right.
No book CQ corresponds to the core.yml assumptions legitimate_value(V) and worthy_goal(G) or to the exception promote_more_effectively(V,A). WAG has no CQ edges to them either.

cq_rows.note: WAG's current text asks only whether another action could also achieve the goal, as the book does. Its exception pattern, realize_more_effectively({G},{A}), says something stronger: another action would achieve the goal MORE effectively. That is the Best-Means question. So the question text fits the book but the pattern does not: an alternative that is merely as good answers the CQ with yes without making the exception true.

premises: Major premise. Book: 'Source E is an expert in subject domain S containing proposition A.' WAG: '{W} is a credible expert on {D}', plus a separate premise '{S} is a matter of {D}'. WAG folds the Expertise CQ ('credible') into the premise and splits off domain membership. The split matches version IV, which has separate Expertise and Field Premises.
Minor premise. Book: 'E asserts that proposition A (in domain S) is true (false).' WAG: '{W} says that {S}'. WAG drops the negative reading, '(false)'.
The variable letters clash. In the book S is the DOMAIN and A the proposition; in WAG S is the proposition and D the domain.

WAG's carneades_id is credible_source (Wyner 2016), not walton.yml expert_opinion (Walton 1997). expert_opinion's loci follow the book's p. 33 burdens one to one, with based_on_evidence as an assumption.
AS:expert_opinion.conclusion: Book (1997): 'A may plausibly be taken to be true (false).' Book (2002, p. 91): 'A is true (false).' WAG: '{S}'. WAG drops 'plausibly' and the (false) form.

cq_rows.note: WAG adds the domain ('on {D}'). Both WAG and the draft treat it as a premise (p. 33: an implicit premise).
cq_rows.book_text: How credible is E as an expert source?
cq_rows.wag_text: How credible is {W} as an expert on {D}?

cq_rows.note: The two ask different things. The book asks whether the EXPERT's field is A's field. WAG asks whether the CLAIM belongs to D. Because WAG split the premise, its field CQ covers only the claim-in-D part, and whether W is an expert in D falls under CQ:expertise. Together, the two WAG CQs cover the book's question.
cq_rows.book_text: Is E an expert in the field that A is in?
cq_rows.wag_text: Is {S} really a matter of {D}?

cq_rows.note: The two ask different things. The book's question is open: 'What did E assert that implies A?'. Subquestions 3.1-3.4 cover quotation, inference and interpretation. WAG's question is yes/no: did W really say S. That is the shape of the position-to-know CQ3, and it loses the indirect 'implies'.
cq_rows.book_text: What did E assert that implies A?
cq_rows.wag_text: Did {W} really say that {S}?

cq_rows.note: The book asks 'Is E personally reliable as a source?', with three subquestions: biased? honest? conscientious? WAG's current text asks only two of them, honest and unbiased; it drops 'personally reliable' and 'conscientious'. WAG's edge targets only biased({W}). credible_source in core.yml also has the exception dishonest(W), but no CQ edge reaches it for this scheme, although the WAG question mentions honesty. Both WAG and the draft treat the CQ as an exception (p. 33).
cq_rows.book_text: Is E personally reliable as a source?
cq_rows.wag_text: Is {W} honest and unbiased?
cq_rows.wag_text_at_HEAD_cbf69b3: Is {W} reliable as a source, honest and unbiased?

cq_rows.note: Two wording differences. The book compares with other experts, WAG with other credible sources. The book asks whether A is CONSISTENT with them, WAG whether they AGREE. Sources can be consistent with A by saying nothing about it, so a 'no' to WAG's question need not mean that they disagree. Yet WAG's exception pattern is other_credible_sources_disagree({S}). Both treat the CQ as an exception. The book (p. 33) also calls it 'a rebuttal', so conclusion is the alternative.
cq_rows.book_text: Is A consistent with what other experts assert?
cq_rows.wag_text: Do other credible sources agree that {S}?
cq_rows.wag_text_at_HEAD_cbf69b3: Is {S} consistent with what other credible sources assert?

cq_rows.note: The meaning is the same. The loci differ. WAG uses argument (an undercutter). On p. 33 the book treats this CQ as an implicit premise, i.e. an assumption the proponent must support. On p. 92 it groups CQs 5 and 6 as attacks on 'the link between premises and conclusion', which supports WAG's choice. The two passages disagree.

premises: Major premise. Book: 'Source a is in a position to know about things in a certain subject domain S containing proposition A.' The p. 17 form instead reads 'a is in a position to know whether A is true (false).', with no domain at all.

premises: Book version 1: 'Major Premise: Generally, case C1 is similar to case C2.' / 'Minor Premise: Proposition A is true (false) in case C1.' WAG: '{C} is a similar case' / '{A} is true in the case of {C}'.
WAG has only one case variable, the source; the target case is left implicit.
WAG drops 'Generally', the defeasibility marker, and (false).
Book version 2 adds a 'Relevant Similarity Premise' (p. 58); WAG has none. The book recommends version 1 and reserves version 2 for cases where relevance must be decided (p. 86).
